schools.summary: Gill takes the sickness for a disease sent in punishment of the father's sin, and is particular about the loaves and the pricked cakes.
Henry presses the aim of the stroke, that sinners must bend or break, and turns the disguise against the man who credited the prophet with seeing the future.
Clarke reads the sickness as both a prelude to the family's ruin and a merciful warning meant to turn the king from his idolatry.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the blind eyes from the phrase used of cataract and the choice of prophet from the king's own history; Ellicott supplies what Shiloh had become and the risk in the gift.

debates.question: Why did the king send to this prophet of all men?

sides.position: Because he had slighted the earlier admonition and expected no favourable answer, yet this was the man whose word about the throne had come true
Because men who disqualify themselves for comfort still expect their ministers to speak peace

outliers.note: Alone in noticing that the sons of Jeroboam and of Rehoboam bore the same name, and in asking whether that is more than coincidence.

themes: Abijah fell sick
disguise thyself
get thee to Shiloh
ten loaves and cracknels
1.pericope_label: Abijah fell sick; get thee to Shiloh to Ahijah the prophet

schools.summary: Gill credits the wife with obedience and affection, allows either a dream or an impulse as the channel of the warning, and reckons the rent portion at ten parts of twelve.
Henry fastens on the title the Lord God of Israel, makes the recital of mercies an argument against ingratitude, and measures the king against David's unbroken adherence to God's worship.
Clarke supplies the unstated motive for the disguise and insists God permitted the rending rather than performed it.

Keil and Delitzsch render the preamble and gloss the phrase for casting God behind the back as the strict opposite of keeping him before the eyes; Ellicott traces the idiom for eyes set to the look of the iris under cataract.

debates.question: In what sense were the calves other gods, if they honoured the God of the exodus?

sides.position: Because they were worshipped as the heathen worshipped theirs, changed the truth of God into a lie, and left ignorant worshippers stopping at the image
Because making them was a breach of an express command, set against the standard of David

outliers.note: Alone in defending the charge of outdoing all predecessors by comparison, that Saul never worshipped idols and Solomon never made Israel to sin.

themes: why feignest thou thyself to be another
I exalted thee from among the people
thou hast not been as my servant David
cast me behind thy back
4.pericope_label: Why feignest thou thyself to be another? I made thee prince over my people

schools.summary: Gill defends the comparison against David, Saul and Solomon, and allows the clause may look only at previous kings of Israel.
Clarke disposes of the blunt Hebrew idiom in a line, that it means every male wherever it occurs.
Ellicott states the objection from the Judges and the wilderness calf, answers it from effect rather than act, and works the antithesis of the shut up and the left loose.

debates.question: How can this idolatry be worse than all that went before?

sides.position: By comparison of persons: worse than David, than Saul who never gave in to idolatry, than Solomon who never drew the people in
By aggravation, since a special promise given on the sole condition of obedience was held in contempt
By effect, since other idolatries passed away while this one went on poisoning the springs of national faith

outliers.note: Alone in raising the ancient belief that denying burial injured the departed soul, and in grounding the repugnance at an outrage on the dead in the law's honouring of the body.

themes: him that dieth in the city the dogs shall eat
him that is shut up and him that is left
as a man taketh away dung
the house of Jeroboam
9.pericope_label: Thou hast done evil above all that were before thee

schools.summary: Gill explains the national mourning from the boy's being a hopeful heir on whom expectations for religion rested, and names Baasha as the king to be raised up.
Clarke draws the general rule, that God will not destroy the righteous with the wicked and respects even a seed of good.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the ellipsis in the closing words and note the emphasis thrown onto the last phrase; Ellicott collects the divergent renderings and prefers the English.

debates.question: What do the closing words of the verse mean?

sides.position: God will raise up such a king this day; and then, but what do I say, he has raised him up even now
In that day; but what say I, the judgment is even now at hand

outliers.note: Alone in asking how the Old Testament as a whole regards an early death, and in concluding that life is treated throughout as a place of God's favour which only wilful sin turns to sorrow.

themes: the child shall die
all Israel shall mourn for him
there is found some good thing
a king over Israel
12.pericope_label: The child shall die; all Israel shall mourn for him

schools.summary: Gill takes the reed of political instability, the kingdom passing from family to family through civil wars, and his note on the cause of the ruin is four words.
Clarke supplies the historical terminus instead, the destruction of the whole house and posterity of Jeroboam by Baasha.

Keil and Delitzsch unpack the compressed Hebrew of the swaying reed and the Mosaic language of the banishment; Ellicott carries the figure through to the uprooting and writes the chapter's longest note on Asherah.

debates.question: What is the reed shaken in the water?

sides.position: Political instability, the throne passing from family to family with no settled peace
A swaying to and fro under a strong wind, with no hold firm enough to resist the storm
The reed uprooted, swept down the stream and cast ashore at a distance, which is the exile

outliers.note: Alone in entering a caution that a prophecy once uttered does not foreclose the probation of later ages, citing the declaration in Jeremiah.

themes: as a reed is shaken in the water
root up Israel out of this good land
because they have made their groves
he shall give Israel up
15.pericope_label: The LORD shall smite Israel as a reed is shaken in the water

schools.summary: Gill has the child buried honourably as his pedigree required, supplies the wars that are known, and reckons the twenty-two years against the neighbouring reigns.
Henry finds nothing good to say of Rehoboam and lists five facts against him, including the warning he draws from the Ammonitess mother about being unequally yoked.
Clarke simply refers the reader to Chronicles for the important particulars.

Ellicott makes the mention of Tirzah do historical work and characterises the first sixty years of the two kingdoms; Keil and Delitzsch date the new king's birth and read the chosen city as a contrast to his idolatry.

debates.question: Why does the record say so little about the rest of the reign?

sides.position: Because the historian cares only for the exaltation, the promise, the idolatry and its punishment, and folds the rest into two phrases
Because of the wars themselves only the campaign against Abijam left any account in the annals

outliers.note: Alone in attributing Rehoboam's character to Solomon's late defection, which did more to corrupt him than the earlier wisdom and devotion had done to ground him.

themes: the child died
he was buried, and all Israel mourned
the rest of the acts of Jeroboam
Rehoboam reigned in Judah
17.pericope_label: The child died; Rehoboam reigned in Judah

schools.summary: Gill identifies the men by the vice named from the men of Sodom, reports a Jewish reading of adultery, and notes that such practices commonly attended heathen idolatry.
Clarke's gloss is etymological, consecrated persons devoted in the greatest impurity to the service of the most impure idols.

Keil and Delitzsch reconstruct the three good years from Chronicles and explain that the monuments were memorial stones originally dedicated to Jehovah; Ellicott describes the pillars and stumps and traces the ban on them.

debates.question: Who is to blame for this apostasy?

sides.position: The people at large, this king being too weak to take the initiative in good or evil
The influence of Solomon's idolatry, under which these young men grew up
The king himself, who followed the law earnestly at first and then let the reaction pass

outliers.note: Alone in arguing from principle that sins committed in a more advanced state of knowledge are worse in guilt than those of a semi-barbarous age.

themes: Judah did evil in the sight of the LORD
high places, and images, and groves
on every high hill, and under every green tree
sodomites in the land
22.pericope_label: Judah did evil; they built them high places

schools.summary: Gill fixes the date, supposes the treasures were both motive and intelligence through Jeroboam's Egyptian intimacy, and identifies the hoard as David's dedication for the temple.
Clarke calls it the most immense booty ever acquired in one place and recalls the three hundred shields of beaten gold.

Keil and Delitzsch summarise the campaign from Chronicles and point to the Karnak bas-relief with its captive figures; Ellicott treats the same inscription as confirmation and reads the silence about a sack of the city.

debates.question: What does the verse imply about how Jerusalem fell?

sides.position: A surrender of the city and its treasures, since there is no notice of a sack, no desecration of the Temple, not even a stripping of its decorations
A campaign that took all the fortified cities and reached the capital, broken off only when the king and the chiefs humbled themselves

outliers.note: Alone in drawing a critical conclusion, that the theory of an invasion destroying all ancient monuments and archives has no support here, and the datings built on it must go with it.

themes: Shishak king of Egypt came up
he took away the treasures
the shields of gold which Solomon had made
all were carried away
25.pericope_label: Shishak came up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures

schools.summary: Gill explains the brass as plain necessity, allows the king his temple-going for all his idolatry, and splits the difference on the war by distinguishing offensive from defensive.

Clarke calculates the guard at three hundred to match the shields, and draws from the apostate father and heathen mother the reflection that righteousness cannot be propagated while unrighteousness may.

Keil and Delitzsch argue from the silence that the war denotes only hostile attitude, and work the older form of the son's name as father of the sea; Ellicott reads the brass as a deliberate symbol and is the most cautious about the war.

debates.question: What is meant by the war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam?

sides.position: Only the hostile feeling and attitude of the two rulers, since no open war is recorded and the attack had been forbidden
A defensive war of border skirmishes, the offensive one being what the prophet forbade
Perhaps only a continued enmity that broke off peaceful relations, with certainty not to be had

outliers.note: Alone in reporting the textual spread of the son's name from Kennicott and De Rossi, with the form of the gospel genealogy supported by thirteen manuscripts and thirteen editions.

themes: shields of brass
the guard bare them
war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam
Abijam his son reigned in his stead
27.pericope_label: Rehoboam made shields of brass; war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam
